days.title: Classification & Taxonomy
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define taxonomy and systematics.
  • Describe the hierarchical classification system.
  • Apply binomial nomenclature.
  • Explain the 3-domain and 5-kingdom schemes.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Taxonomy — science of naming and classifying organisms.
  • Systematics — study of evolutionary relationships.
  • Binomial nomenclature — two-part naming (Genus species).
  • Domain — largest taxonomic rank.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Hierarchical Classification

Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species

B. Binomial Nomenclature

  • Developed by Linnaeus
  • Genus capitalized, species lowercase
  • Both italicized
  • Example: Homo sapiens

C. Classification Schemes

SchemeGroups
3-DomainBacteria, Archaea, Eukarya
5-KingdomMonera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia

D. Why 3-Domain is Preferred

Molecular evidence (rRNA) shows Archaea and Bacteria are fundamentally different.

scenarios.text: The scientific name Homo sapiens is written:
The largest taxonomic rank is:
Which domains are prokaryotic?
Which kingdom is NOT in the 3-domain scheme?
Which rank is the most specific?
Human classification: Homo sapiens belongs to:

questions.text: Which is the correct way to write a species name?
Which domains are in the 3-domain system?

takeaways: Taxonomy names & classifies; systematics studies relationships.
Hierarchy: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
3-Domain is preferred based on molecular evidence.

days.title: Taxa & Distinctive Characteristics
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define taxon.
  • Identify distinctive characteristics of major taxa.
  • Compare members of different kingdoms.
  • Explain how DNA helps classify organisms.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Taxon — any group at any taxonomic level.
  • Distinctive characteristics — features that distinguish a taxon.
  • Molecular taxonomy — uses DNA sequences.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Major Kingdoms

KingdomDistinctive Features
Monera (Bacteria/Archaea)Prokaryotic, no nucleus
ProtistaEukaryotic, mostly unicellular
FungiEukaryotic, chitin cell walls, heterotrophic
PlantaeEukaryotic, cellulose cell walls, autotrophic
AnimaliaEukaryotic, no cell wall, heterotrophic, motile

B. Structural vs Molecular Classification

  • Structural — physical features (morphology)
  • Developmental — embryology
  • Molecular — DNA/protein sequences

C. Example

Some organisms that look similar are genetically very different (convergent evolution), and vice versa.

scenarios.text: Organism has chitin cell walls and is heterotrophic.
Organism has cellulose cell walls and photosynthesizes.
Organism has no cell wall and moves.
Organism is prokaryotic.
Unicellular eukaryote.
Two organisms look alike but are genetically different.

questions.text: Which kingdom has NO cell wall?
Which is used to classify organisms by evolutionary relationships?

takeaways: Taxa are groups at any taxonomic level.
Structural, developmental, and molecular data help classify organisms.
Molecular data can reveal hidden relationships.

days.title: Species Diversity & Cladistics
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define species diversity.
  • Explain cladistics.
  • Differentiate ancestral from derived traits.
  • Identify shared derived characteristics.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Species diversity — variety of species in an ecosystem.
  • Cladistics — grouping by shared derived characteristics.
  • Ancestral trait — primitive trait shared with distant ancestors.
  • Derived trait — new trait unique to a group.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Species Diversity

  • Species richness — number of species
  • Species evenness — how evenly distributed
  • Highest in tropical rainforests

B. Cladistics

Groups organisms based on shared derived characteristics (synapomorphies). A clade includes an ancestor and all its descendants.

C. Trait Types

Trait TypeMeaning
Ancestral (plesiomorphy)Old trait, shared broadly
Derived (apomorphy)New trait, unique to a group
SynapomorphyShared derived trait

scenarios.text: An ecosystem has 500 species.
A trait is unique to mammals.
A trait is shared by all vertebrates.
Grouping organisms by shared derived traits.
A clade includes:
Highest species diversity is in:

takeaways: Cladistics groups by shared derived traits.

days.title: Building & Interpreting Cladograms
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Construct a simple cladogram.
  • Interpret nodes and branches.
  • Identify monophyletic groups.
  • Compare cladistics with traditional taxonomy.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cladogram — branching diagram of relationships.
  • Node — common ancestor point.
  • Monophyletic group — ancestor + all descendants.
  • Outgroup — reference taxon outside the study group.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Constructing a Cladogram

  1. Choose the group of interest
  2. Choose an outgroup
  3. Identify shared derived traits
  4. Group by shared derived traits

B. Reading a Cladogram

  • Nodes = common ancestors
  • Branches = lineages
  • Tips = species or groups
  • Character changes marked on branches

C. Example

Vertebrate cladogram: Fish → Amphibians → Reptiles → Birds → Mammals. Traits: jaws, lungs, amniotic egg, feathers, hair.
